faq.a: Muscle power grading combined with reflex testing; absent reflex points to nerve involvement.
faq.q: What bedside test helps differentiate nerve from muscle injury?

faq.a: High CK (>1000 U/L) indicates rhabdomyolysis, which can cause acute kidney injury and needs aggressive hydration.
faq.q: Why is CK important in a patient with malaria?

faq.a: If there is suspicion of compartment syndrome, abscess requiring drainage, or unstable fracture.
faq.q: When is a referral for surgery indicated?

exam: A 25‑year‑old with sickle‑cell disease presents with unilateral thigh pain and swelling – what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Perform a focused exam and obtain a plain X‑ray to rule out bone infarction; CK helps assess rhabdomyolysis.

A patient on antiretroviral therapy develops calf tenderness and dark urine – which investigation is essential and what does it guide? — Check CK; a markedly raised level confirms rhabdomyolysis and dictates aggressive IV fluids.

Foot drop is noted in a farmer after stepping on a sharp object – which nerve is likely injured and what immediate management is required? — Common peroneal nerve; immobilise the ankle in dorsiflexion and arrange physiotherapy.

A child with malaria complains of leg pain; how do you differentiate simple myalgia from dangerous rhabdomyolysis? — Measure CK; >1000 U/L warrants fluid resuscitation and monitoring of renal function.

In a patient with HIV, bilateral quadriceps wasting is observed – what are the top three differential diagnoses? — HIV‑associated myopathy, opportunistic infection (e.g., TB myositis), antiretroviral toxicity.

During ward rounds you find a patient with a swollen calf, fever, and a positive rapid malaria test – what is the priority treatment and why? — Start ACT for malaria and give IV fluids to prevent renal injury from possible rhabdomyolysis.

A young adult presents with sudden inability to extend the knee after a road‑traffic accident – what structure is most likely damaged and what is the first step? — Quadriceps tendon rupture; immobilise the knee in extension and arrange surgical repair.
Why should NSAIDs be avoided in a patient with severe malaria and leg swelling? — They can worsen renal impairment and mask fever, complicating assessment of infection severity.
ai.title: Leg Muscles
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: An overview of the major muscles of the lower limb, their actions, innervation and common clinical problems seen in low‑resource settings. Emphasises bedside assessment and relevant differentials.

b: Quadriceps (knee extension) – femoral nerve
Hamstrings (knee flexion, hip extension) – sciatic nerve
Calf (gastrocnemius, soleus) – tibial nerve
Adductors – obturator nerve
sections.p: The lower limb contains three functional muscle groups: anterior (flexors), posterior (extensors) and medial (adductors). They are supplied by the femoral, sciatic and obturator nerves respectively.

b: Power 3/5 = active movement against gravity
Absent knee‑jerk suggests L3‑L4 radiculopathy or femoral nerve lesion
Foot drop = tibial nerve or L4‑L5 root problem
sections.p: Muscle power is graded 0‑5, and tendon reflexes help localise nerve injury. In low‑resource hospitals, simple bedside tests replace EMG.

b: Tuberculous osteomyelitis of the femur → quadriceps wasting
Malaria‑related rhabdomyolysis → calf tenderness, dark urine
Sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusive crisis → thigh muscle infarction
Herbal poultices → cellulitis and secondary abscess
sections.p: Common presentations include painful limp, swelling, and weakness. Tropical infections, trauma and malnutrition are frequent causes.

t.b: Identify pattern of weakness and pain; distinguishes nerve vs muscle disease
Detect fractures, osteomyelitis, bone infarcts; if unavailable, rely on clinical signs
Elevated >1000 U/L suggests rhabdomyolysis; normal does not rule out neuropathy
Positive in febrile patients with muscle pain; treat promptly
Positive results raise suspicion for opportunistic myositis or neuropathy

b: Antibiotics for bacterial myositis/abscess (e.g., ceftriaxone) – avoid penicillin if allergy
Antimalarials for malaria‑related muscle injury – ACT preferred, avoid quinine in G6PD deficiency
Analgesia with paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs if renal impairment
Physiotherapy: active‑assisted range‑of‑motion, progressive strengthening
Compression bandage for swelling; elevate limb
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, protect the limb and restore function.

b: Weakness isolated to knee extension → quadriceps/femoral nerve lesion
Foot drop with preserved knee extension → common peroneal nerve injury
Bilateral calf tenderness in a malaria endemic area → consider rhabdomyolysis
sections.p: Exam questions often test localisation, differential diagnosis and immediate steps.

b: Assuming all leg pain is orthopedic; always assess neurovascular status
Neglecting CK in a febrile patient with muscle pain
Prescribing NSAIDs in severe malaria without checking renal function
sections.p: Pitfalls include over‑reliance on imaging, missing nerve root signs and ignoring tropical infections.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe pain with swelling suggesting compartment syndrome
Fever with leg swelling in an immunocompromised patient
